name: Authorization Conventions
description: This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on authorization so output stays consistent and easy to review.
content:
This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on authorization so output stays consistent and easy to review.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Prefer explicit, readable authorization solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
2. Keep authorization outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
3. Re-check edge cases relevant to authorization (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
4. Check that authorization terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
5. Document any non-obvious authorization decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
6. Measure before optimizing any authorization bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. Prefer the simplest authorization approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
8. State assumptions about authorization explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
9. When multiple authorization strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
10. Keep authorization changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
11. When authorization decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
12. Before starting authorization work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of authorization correctness.
- Avoid mixing unrelated authorization concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not apply generic authorization advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting authorization assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for authorization, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
